description: There are ceremonial and culinary grades of matcha. Ceremonial grade is higher quality, suited for traditional tea ceremonies and drinking straight. Culinary grade is for cooking, smoothies, and lattes.
Usucha is thin matcha. Use about 2g of matcha powder with 70-80ml of 70-80°C water. Whisk quickly in an 'M' or 'W' motion until a fine foam appears.
Koicha is thick matcha. Use about 4g of matcha with 40ml of water. Whisk slowly to avoid foam; the result is a thick, syrup-like tea.
Matcha is rich in catechins (especially EGCG), provides calm energy through L-theanine, and has antioxidants that help support health and focus.
Traditional tools include the Chasen (bamboo whisk), Chawan (bowl), Chashaku (scoop), and Natsume (container).
Uji (Kyoto), Nishio (Aichi), and Shizuoka are famous regions in Japan known for premium matcha production.
Matcha is made by shade-growing tea plants for ~3 weeks, hand-picking young leaves, steaming them, drying, and stone-grinding into fine powder.
Matcha involves consuming the entire tea leaf as powder, offering higher antioxidant levels. Regular green tea is brewed and discarded.
Water too hot burns matcha and makes it bitter. Always use water cooled to about 70-80°C (158-176°F).
To make a matcha latte, whisk 2g matcha with 60ml hot water, then pour over 200ml steamed milk (dairy or plant-based). Sweeten to taste.
Keep matcha in an airtight container, away from light, heat, and moisture to preserve freshness. Refrigeration can extend shelf life.
A formal ritualized practice involving the preparation, serving, and drinking of matcha with specific movements and utensils.
Using boiling water, under-whisking, using too little powder, or improper storage all affect matcha quality negatively.
Matcha's origins trace back to Tang Dynasty China, later perfected in Japan by Zen monks.
Matcha is now popular globally in lattes, ice cream, pastries, and even skincare products.
Blend 1 tsp matcha, 1 banana, 1 cup spinach, 1/2 cup yogurt, and 1 cup almond milk for an energizing green smoothie.
Use a bamboo whisk (chasen) to briskly move the wrist in a 'W' or 'M' motion until fine foam forms for perfect texture.
Usucha is lighter, foamier, and thinner. Koicha is heavier, thicker, and served with less whisking and no foam.
Always sift matcha before whisking to prevent clumping and achieve a smooth, creamy consistency.
Brands like Ippodo, Marukyu Koyamaen, Itohkyuemon, and Matcha.com are well-known for high-quality ceremonial matcha.
